newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-IEA says oil weaker as stock cushion expands.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IEA says oil weaker as stock cushion expands.

text.p: Fast rising world oil supplies and a mild winter have allowed oil companies to replenish lean stocks, putting the skids under crude markets, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.
Accelerating oil output growth looks set to outstrip a strong expansion in world demand, according to figures released in the Paris-based agency's latest monthly oil market report.

"Although weather effects, oilfield delays and technical problems in the North Sea and Australia have restricted oil production from a number of key fields so far this year, supplies from other fields in other areas have more than compensated," the West's energy watchdog said.
Market analysts said they agreed that supplies this year were likely to outweigh oil demand. But they said the IEA had exaggerated the supply outlook, repeating a mistake it made last year.

Global oil output shot up by 2.28 million barrels a day (bpd) in the past four months to 74.8 million bpd, the agency, which draws its membership from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said.
"A substantial relaxation in global supply/demand fundamentals led to a steep decline in ... crude oil prices," it added.
International benchmark Brent blend has fallen more than 20 percent since mid-January -- down $5.25 in that period to $19.65 a barrel by 1300 GMT on Friday.
The IEA said tight oil inventories in the world's leading industrialised nations staged a further recovery in January to end the month higher than a year before for the first time in 18 months.
Commercial stocks in OECD countries were drawn down by a modest 100,000 bpd in January, compared with a million bpd decline in the same month last year.

The IEA is forecasting growth of 1.9 million bpd in world oil demand this year to 73.7 million bpd. But it says countries outside the OPEC producer grouping will pump the required extra volume, leaving no room on oil markets for rising OPEC output.

The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, boosted by the second full month of Iraqi supplies under the U.N.'s oil-for-food exchange, kept output at a high 26.98 million bpd in February, the IEA estimated.
A balanced market needed only 25.4 million bpd of OPEC supply on average this year, it said.

"We think the amount OPEC is producing at the moment is above average demand for the year but the outlook for the market isn't as bad as the IEA figures would suggest," said Mike Barry at Energy Market Consultants.
The agency admitted on Friday that its forecasts had proved wide of the mark for 1996 because of unforeseen events and shortcomings in its methodology.
It said projections for world supply released a year ago had since been revised down by 650,000 bpd, while it had underestimated demand by 310,000 bpd.
Changes in methodology meant "our 1997 projection of demand should be more reliable," its said.
But, in a comparison with other forecasts, the agency was still projecting higher supplies than any of a range of forecasts by 11 independent energy economists.
The IEA's projection for 1.9 million bpd of extra world supply exceeds the average of 11 forecasts by 400,000 bpd and the lowest by a huge 800,000 bpd.
"We think they're making the same errors again this year as last," said Barry at Energy Market Consultants.
